terms.short: A separate location inside a Region, like us-east-2a. Each Region has at least three, so apps can survive one failing.
A geographic area, like Ireland or Tokyo, with at least three Availability Zones. Your resources live where you pick.
Lets CloudFront sign its requests to a private S3 bucket, so only your distribution can read the files.
Time to live: how long a cached copy is kept before it must be checked or fetched again.
JSON web token: a signed token that proves who a user is. Cognito issues them when someone signs in.
How an EC2 instance reads data about itself. Version 2 gets a session token first and sends it with each request.
Virtual private cloud: your own private network in AWS, where you choose the IP ranges, subnets and routes.
A slice of a VPC's IP range that sits in one Availability Zone. Spread subnets over zones to survive one failing.
A stateful firewall around a resource. You list the traffic allowed in or out, and replies are let through.
An identity with permissions that people, services or code take on for a while, using temporary credentials.
Amazon Resource Name: the unique label of every AWS resource, like arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket.
Point-in-time recovery: DynamoDB keeps continuous backups so you can restore a table to any second, up to 35 days back.
Dead-letter queue: where messages go after failing too many times, so you can look at them instead of losing them.
Server-side encryption with keys that S3 manages. Every new object uploaded to S3 gets it automatically.
An encryption key kept in AWS Key Management Service. Key policies and IAM decide who may use it.
An AWS site in a city near your users, where CloudFront keeps cached copies so content arrives faster.
The delay between asking for something and getting the answer, usually measured in milliseconds.
Safe to repeat: sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once.
The extra wait when Lambda sets up a fresh environment before running your code. It happens in under 1% of calls.
The DynamoDB attribute that decides where an item is stored. Reading an item by its key is fast.
Retrieval-augmented generation: the app finds relevant documents first and gives them to the model to ground its answer.
A Bedrock safety filter that checks prompts and answers, blocking harmful content or topics you choose to deny.
Standby copies of a database in other Availability Zones. If the primary fails, a standby takes over automatically.
A read-only copy of a database that keeps in sync, taking read traffic off the main database.
Lets API Gateway reach private resources in your VPC, such as a load balancer, without putting them on the internet.
Application Load Balancer: spreads web requests across healthy targets and can route them by path or host name.
AWS's own Arm-based processors. Lambda functions on them (arm64) can get better price performance.
The language environment your code runs in, such as Node.js or Python. In Lambda, you choose one for each function.
AgentCore's serverless hosting for AI agents and tools. Each user session runs in its own isolated microVM.
AWS's free offer: new accounts get credits to try services, and over 30 services have monthly free usage.
Running a trained model to get an answer, like sending a prompt to a Bedrock model and getting text back.
A JSON permissions document on an S3 bucket that says who can do what with the bucket and its objects.
A JSON document listing which actions are allowed or denied on which resources. Attach it to a user, group or role.
Give each person or role only the permissions its task needs, and nothing more.
Multi-factor authentication: signing in needs a second proof, like a code from an app, as well as a password.
Lets servers in a private subnet reach the internet, while outside services can't start a connection to them.
A VPC's door to the internet. Public subnets route through it so resources with public IPs can reach the internet.
A set of EC2 instances that EC2 Auto Scaling keeps at the size you want, adding or replacing servers as needed.
Content delivery network: servers around the world keep copies of your content close to users. CloudFront is one.
You run code or use a service without managing servers. AWS handles the capacity, and you usually pay per use.
A list of numbers that captures the meaning of text or an image, so similar things end up close together.
A point-in-time copy of data, such as a disk or a database. EBS snapshots save only blocks changed since the last one.
A web application firewall: rules that inspect web requests and block common attacks before they reach your app.
Distributed denial of service: a flood of traffic from many machines trying to knock a site offline. AWS Shield helps.
S3 keeps every version of an object, so you can bring back one that was overwritten or deleted by mistake.
A private connection from your VPC to an AWS service, so the traffic doesn't cross the public internet.
A way to write an IP address range, like 10.0.0.0/16. The number after the slash sets how big the range is.
Proves a site's identity so browsers can connect over HTTPS. AWS Certificate Manager issues them.
Watches a metric and acts when it crosses a line you set, such as emailing you or adding servers.
A number that names a computer on a network, like a street address, so data knows where to go.
The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the IP address of a server.
The locked, private way browsers talk to websites. A certificate proves the site is the real one.
The set of requests one program can send another, like a menu: "give me order 42" or "save this photo".
A language for asking a database questions, like "show me every order from Tuesday".
A safe way to type commands on a faraway Linux server over the internet. It uses port 22.
Remote Desktop Protocol: lets you see and use a faraway Windows server's screen. It uses port 3389.
Access control list: an older way to say who may read or write something, like an S3 object.
Amazon Machine Image: a saved starting copy of a server's disk, used to start new EC2 instances.
Extract, transform, load: pull data out, tidy it up, then save it where it's useful.
Online transaction processing: lots of small, quick reads and writes, like recording each sale in a shop.
Online analytical processing: big questions over lots of data, like total sales for every year.
Teaching a computer to spot patterns from examples, instead of writing every rule by hand.
Integrated development environment: the app programmers write, run and test their code in.
Optical character recognition: software reads the letters in a picture or scan and turns them into text.
A plain text table: one row per line, with commas between the values. Spreadsheets can open it.
